newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends firm in Europe as euro tension lingers.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends firm in Europe as euro tension lingers.

text.p: The dollar ended firm in Europe at Tuesday's closing levels, underpinned by continued confusion about the shape and size of the single European currency and amid expectations of a strong U.S. employment report on Friday.
Dollar sales in the mid-1.73's against the mark earlier kept a lid on the U.S. unit as the row between the Bundesbank and the German finance ministry about its gold reserves seemed to cool.
Analysts said the incident would reverberate for some time, however, and would act as a constant weight on the mark.
"The damage has been done," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago in London.
"Regardless of today's compromise, the feeling in the market is that the German finance ministry is prepared to do pretty much anything to get its deficit in line," said Knuthsen.
Finance Minister Theo "Waigel comes out of this a weaker minister after the incident and this feeds the argument the euro will be a softer currency," he said.
At 1510 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.7295/00 compared with 1.7274/84 late Tuesday. Against the yen, it was little changed at 116.13/23 compared with 116.09/19 late yesterday.
Bonn announced earlier it agreed to compromise with the Bundesbank on the proposed revaluation of reserves in 1997.

The Bundesbank - which railed against the gold plan as compromising its independence - effectively forced Waigel to delay the measures to 1998. German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, however, backed his finance minister today and Waigel survived a parliamentary censure motion.
Kohl then set about soothing jitters about the single currency plan and reiterated Germany's commitment to the budgetary targets and the timetable of January 1, 1999.
Analysts say it will now be difficult for Germany to exclude other EMU hopefuls like Italy from the euro on budgetary grounds and a broad-based start to the project could undermine the unit.

A broad-based starting membership to monetary union has also been made more likely this week by the new Socialist government in France, which publicly advocates the inclusion of as many countries as possible.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer later helped support the mark, which is suffering from the prospect of being replaced by a currency less stable than itself, by stating he favoured a strong German currency in the future.
The fragile German economy, however, will make that a difficult task in the months ahead. German industrial production fell 1.3 percent during the month of April.

This again stands in contrast to the relative buoyancy of the U.S. economy, which is expected to report another robust employment report for May on Friday. Analysts polled by Reuters expect a 221,000 rise in non-farm payrolls during the month.
News today of a bigger-than-expected 1.2 percent rise in April factory goods orders helped kep the picture rosy.
"The dollar yields more (than the mark), its got a bubbling economy, no inflation and a certain future," said one trader at a UK fund management firm. "What more do you need?"
The Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee meets on July 1 and 2 to discuss the possibility of another interest rate rise.

Dollar/yen wobbled in late trading here as the head of the U.S. National Association of Manufacturers Jerry Jasinowski said the dollar above 110 yen was a problem. Currency traders, however, feel the U.S. and Japan have a comfort zone about 115.

Sterling/mark had a roller-coaster day, piggy-backing the dollar/mark to its highest level since August 1992 before recoiling sharply after Bank of England governor Eddie George talked of its "exaggerated strength."
The new Bank of England policy-making council meets Thursday amid some expectations of another quarter-point UK rate rise.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
